vignette:
He was on tour last fall, driving through the mountains in a rented van after a show in Medellín. The roads were dark, wet from a sudden storm, and the driver—his bassist—took a curve too fast. The van slid, spun twice, and slammed into a guardrail, then tipped onto its side. He remembers the sound of metal folding, glass shattering like a cymbal dropped from a great height. He remembers the smell of gasoline and wet earth, and the terrible silence after the van stopped moving. He was pinned in the backseat for forty-five minutes, his right leg trapped under a collapsed amplifier, while the rain came in through the broken window and soaked his face.

Now, six months later, he still cannot drive at night, especially in the rain. His wife does most of the errands, even if it means she has to leave work early. He tells himself it is practical, but the truth is that every time he sits behind the wheel, his chest tightens and his palms sweat, and sometimes he has to pull over because his vision blurs. He has not told her about the images that flash behind his eyes without warning: the headlights sweeping across the road, the guardrail rushing toward him, the sound of his own voice screaming—a recording he never knew he had made.

He still plays guitar. That part of his life remains intact, like a room in a house that the storm somehow missed. He is booked for a small festival next month, and when he practices, the music is the only thing that feels real. But even there, something has changed. He used to love the loud, crowded clubs; now he stands with his back to the wall, scanning the doors, noticing every flicker of light as anxiety ripples through him. He has started checking the fire exits at every venue before he goes on stage. He does not tell the band why. They think he is being professional.

At home, he is quieter than before. His wife says he seems absent, like he is listening to a song only he can hear. She does not know that when she turns off the lamp at night, he is back in the overturned van, trapped and waiting, his heart hammering against his ribs. He has trouble sleeping—falls asleep, then jolts awake at around 3 a.m., gasping, convinced that something is wrong, that the room is tilted, that the car is still sliding. He gets up, walks through the apartment, touches the walls to steady himself. He has avoided driving that mountain road ever since, even though it is the most direct route to his mother’s house. He takes the long way, an extra hour, and does not tell anyone why.

His PCL-5 score is 44, which means moderate to severe symptoms. But he does not know that number. He knows only that he feels hollowed out, that his memory of the accident comes in fragments—a sleeve of rain, the metal taste of blood, the paramedic’s voice asking if he can feel his toes. He knows that he feels jumpy when he hears a car horn, and that he cannot stand the smell of gasoline. He knows that he used to write songs about love and loss, and now the only lyrics that come are about falling, about being pinned, about waking up in a place that is not quite home.

He is a musician, so he understands rhythm and repetition. He recognizes that his mind keeps playing the same broken chord over and over again, the same crash, the same silence afterward. He just does not know how to change the key.
